stories.topic: Recording with Larry White on Free Banking
stories.summary: Amit recorded an episode of The Seen and the Unseen with Larry White in Washington DC, calling it a masterclass on free banking. From Larry White's book A Clash of Economic Ideas, Amit quotes the Hayek/Keynes-inspired image of an idea-producing factory: high-level researchers produce abstract ideas, applied researchers turn them into less abstract policy ideas, journalists and intellectuals embody them in mass-market books and op-eds, and they reach policymakers and the public.
stories.insight: The 'commercial forest to furniture' metaphor still organises how knowledge moves into society, even though parts of the pipeline are broken. Anyone trying to influence the world has to understand which stage of the supply chain they are operating in.

stories.topic: Why Indian Researchers Have to Contort to Publish Abroad
stories.summary: Indian social science research is routinely told by foreign journals that it 'is not interesting' because it is about India. An obscure SEC regulation change in the United States is publishable in top finance journals; the dramatic activism of SEBI, arguably the world's most activist financial regulator, is dismissed. Indian researchers have to perform an exhausting gymnastics of dressing local insights as Western lessons, framing 'natural experiments in my country' that 'shed light on the grand questions of the age as seen in Germany.'
stories.insight: A wholesale critique of academic localism dressed as universalism. Ajay's prescription: open the windows of your house and look at the real world around you, identify the great questions of your age in your lived experience, and then 'deliver those jewels to the world.' Otherwise the contortion eats the life of the researcher.

stories.topic: George Simenon: No Two People Can Ever Communicate
stories.summary: Amit shares an observation he uses in his writing course: every student carries deep knowledge of some field, acquired through years of education or work, and we learn many difficult things easily. Yet we fail every day at the most basic task of all, communicating. He cites his favourite novelist Georges Simenon, who said the key theme of all his work is that 'no two people can ever communicate with each other.' The puzzle: why do humans, who are born communicating (the cry of a newborn baby is communication), fail at it as adults?
stories.insight: Learning is one variable (you), but communication has two variables (you and the other), and most writers ignore the second. Writing is not putting what is in your head onto a screen; it only becomes meaningful when it has an intended effect on the intended reader.

stories.summary: Amit recalls Malcolm Gladwell's Outliers — research showing that elite athletes are disproportionately born in the first three or four months of the year. The mechanism: in age-group sports, cohorts are determined by 1 January, so a January-born twelve-year-old is substantially more developed than a December-born twelve-year-old, gets selected, gets practice, and the feedback loop compounds into adult ability. Amit notes wryly that his surname starts with V and he is born in December: 'I had no chance.'
stories.insight: Small initial advantages compound through feedback loops into large structural disparities. The category extends beyond sports — alphabetical author conventions in academia (Hayek, Friedman, Keynes, Arrow all front-loaded) and many other apparently trivial sortings can shape who becomes famous.

stories.topic: Mendel Ordered Forty Copies of His Paper
stories.summary: Ajay recalls the trivia from the Outlaws episode: Gregor Mendel, in the pre-electronic era, ordered forty copies of his paper from the printer to disseminate his work. In the modern world there is no such limitation, and yet the world is deluged with too much rubbish, so the lonely researcher's 'treasured child' on a website is unfortunately not waited for and not easy to get read.
stories.insight: The dissemination problem has changed shape, not gone away. Mendel had a printing-cost ceiling; the modern researcher has an attention-floor. Either way, post-production work — videos, blog articles, small intense conferences — is a non-optional part of the craft.

stories.topic: The Apprentice Who Brings a Perfect Slideshow
stories.summary: On Ajay's research teams, papers are developed as a gory internal slideshow (forty to fifty slides, dense data, all tables and citations). The team meets, twenty new ideas come up, and the assistants — typically apprentices — go away to implement them. The challenge for the apprentice is not to dumbly take instructions but to come back at the next meeting with what she believes is an absolutely perfect product, no blemish, ready to defend the paper. If you are just dumbly taking instructions, 'you should not be in research.'
stories.insight: Apprenticeship in a craft is not subservience; it is the practice of taking ownership earlier than your title justifies. The apprentice who shows up ready to defend the paper becomes the journeyman; the one who only takes orders never becomes a master.

stories.topic: The Cute Title That Drags You In But Doesn't Deliver
stories.summary: Ajay confesses he has been pulled back to one paper several times over years by 'a very cute title' that lingers — but the paper itself was 'not the title, just a cute title.' He sees an over-correction in modern academic culture toward enigmatic, literary titles disconnected from the actual work. Amit counter-offers a title he loves: Bijou Rao's early-1990s paper on dowry, 'The Rising Price of Husbands' — clever and accurately about the paper.
stories.insight: A title is the one-sentence summary of a paper that 100,000 people will read. A literary flourish helps, but the title must be about the paper. Cuteness without fidelity is a trap that makes the writer look clever and the reader feel cheated.

stories.topic: Susan Thomas Comes Second Only Because of the Alphabet
stories.summary: Ajay's most frequent co-author is Susan Thomas. Citations always read 'Shah and Thomas,' which makes him sound like the lead. The truth is that economists conventionally list authors alphabetically — 'her work or role is in no way inferior to mine; it's just because.' Ajay's mental model: the only conflict is whether you get equity or not — once everyone is at equity, the alphabetical convention kills all the silly status fights about ordering, the 'n factorial combinations' of who deserves which position.
stories.insight: Conventions are not neutral, but neither are they status statements. The alphabetical convention solves a coordination problem and prevents endless co-author politics. Read other people's authorship orders charitably; don't infer hierarchy from sequence.

recommendations.item: Larry White on Free Banking (The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Larry White
recommendations.context: An episode of The Seen and the Unseen released earlier the same week, recorded in DC.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterclass on free banking, with great novel insights from White, who is an expert in the field. The episode is also the source of the Hayek/Keynes-inspired 'idea factory' framing that opens this conversation.

recommendations.creator: Lawrence H. White
recommendations.context: Larry White's history of twentieth-century economic ideas and policy.
recommendations.reason: Source of the long quotation that frames the episode — the production pipeline from lonely researchers to applied researchers to journalists to policymakers and the public, modelled on commercial forests turning into furniture.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and others
recommendations.context: A peer-reviewed research blog co-edited by Ajay.
recommendations.reason: Held up as an example of writing that fits the IMRD (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) structure — a 'low-bullshit way to do scientific communication' that takes good modern scientific work directly to readers without journal gatekeeping.

recommendations.creator: Vijayendra Rao
recommendations.context: An early-1990s paper studying the changing dowry system.
recommendations.reason: Held up by Amit as one of his favourite paper titles — 'clever and about the paper.' A model for the discipline of titles that are simultaneously memorable and accurate.

recommendations.creator: Malcolm Gladwell
recommendations.context: Gladwell's book of case studies in success.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'birthday effect' research showing elite athletes cluster in the first months of the year because of age-group cut-offs. A vivid illustration of how small initial advantages compound through feedback loops.

recommendations.creator: William Strunk Jr. and E.B. White
recommendations.context: The classic short guide to English usage and writing style.
recommendations.reason: Recommended as universal knowledge for anyone in research. Ajay's view: every researcher who claims to be doing 'fancy econometrics' or computer science but neglects writing has missed the core of the craft.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.reason: Ajay's second recommendation for researchers: people who care about craft should attend it. Reciprocal endorsement of the discipline that this episode is at heart about.

recommendations.item: Economical Writing: Thirty-Five Rules for Clear and Concise Prose
recommendations.creator: Deirdre McCloskey
recommendations.context: McCloskey's manual on writing about complex subjects clearly.
recommendations.reason: Approaches writing from the angle of how to communicate economics — or any technical subject — to readers who don't already know the field. A wonderful book about treating readers with respect.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous episode of EIE on heretics and mavericks.
recommendations.reason: The source of the Mendel-orders-forty-copies trivia and the discussion of figures (Semmelweis, Mendel, Darwin) who would never have survived modern peer review — referenced repeatedly to ground today's argument that peer review systematically rejects path-breaking work.

recommendations.item: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on the broken pipeline between academia and society.
recommendations.reason: The framing of academia as 'a circle jerk game with academics talking to each other, writing on obscure subjects, following fashions of the day' was set up there. This episode picks up the thread of how a paper actually moves through that pipeline.

core_ideas.concept: The Three Elements of a Paper: Question, Answer, Novelty
core_ideas.explanation: Every paper in the STEM and social-science worlds must satisfy three tests. There must be clarity on a question — the writer has to articulate what is being asked. There must be a persuasive answer — not random claims to be believed on the writer's authority but a substantiated case. And it must be novel — not a synthesis of what others have done, however useful that may be. A summary of twenty papers (something an LLM can do) is not a paper. The three tests are also the spine of peer review: the reviewer should restate the question, restate the answer, and judge whether the answer is supported and novel.
core_ideas.quote: What's the question? Is the answer persuasive? And, the third test — is it novel?

core_ideas.concept: The Atom of Knowledge Is Not a Journal Paper
core_ideas.explanation: A paper, properly understood, is a unit of knowledge — a building block — not a journal-published artefact. It can be a working paper, a blog article, a newspaper piece, a peer-reviewed article. The historical role of journals as dissemination mechanism is 100% gone: there is ample remarkably high-quality novel knowledge being published as working papers and blogs. Journals now serve only as career credentials — a brand-name marker that helps you get a job or grant. We are back to the eighteenth-century Royal Society's 'every-to-every' communication model, just without the secretary in the middle.
core_ideas.quote: We are back to the Royal Society and its unstructured dissemination mechanisms... All these concepts are obsolete.

core_ideas.concept: The Importance of a Question Is in the Eye of the Beholder
core_ideas.explanation: Gatekeepers love to declare that some questions are 'important' and others aren't — global warming yes, the headgear of tribals in Chandrapur no. Ajay refuses the snobbery: researchers don't allocate their time foolishly. If somebody is willing to put in the work, third parties should be respectful. Many breakthroughs (the Mavericks of the Outlaws episode) were dismissed by establishments who couldn't see why anyone was wasting time on a 'minor' question. The discipline is to be slow with the judgment that something is unimportant.
core_ideas.quote: There is also the radical possibility that the headgear of the Chandrapur tribals causes global warming.

core_ideas.concept: Two Default Paper Structures: IMRD and the Economics Recipe
core_ideas.explanation: IMRD — Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion — is the STEM default. The Introduction summarises what is known and poses the questions; Methods describes what was done at a level allowing replication; Results presents the numerical findings without too much interpretation; Discussion asks why it matters and what new pathways open up. The economics recipe is similar but more layered: a thousand-word executive summary called 'Introduction' (often published separately as a newspaper piece), then a fresh field-and-questions section, methods, results, robustness checks against alternative hypotheses, and a conclusion that summarises and looks downstream. Both are scaffolds, not straitjackets — the experienced writer can break them when the work demands it.
core_ideas.quote: It is a good way to channel the mind.

core_ideas.concept: Push the Story Aside: The Paper Is Not the Journey
core_ideas.explanation: Doing research is climbing a mountain — fumbling, false starts, three months wasted, an aha moment, serendipity. When you write the paper you have to push all of that aside. The reader does not want your life story; they want a clean question, a clean approach, a clean finding. A successful paper is the act of stepping back from your own lived experience and translating it into a product that stands on its own. The journey is not the destination, and the writer's job is to deliver the destination.
core_ideas.quote: When you're doing the work, you should think it's a journey, not the destination, but when you present the work, it's a destination, not the journey.

core_ideas.concept: Communication Has Two Variables, Learning Has One
core_ideas.explanation: Learning a difficult subject is hard but tractable because there is only one variable — you. Communication is exponentially harder because there are two variables — you and the reader — and most writers ignore the second. The act of writing a paper is not putting what is in your head onto the screen; the paper only becomes meaningful when it has an intended effect on the intended reader. This is why even technically brilliant researchers can produce papers that nobody reads. Writing is fundamentally a craft of empathy.
core_ideas.quote: We were all sitting with our loved one and you could realize that shit, we don't even know each other.

core_ideas.concept: If It Was Not Hard to Write, It Will Not Be Easy to Read
core_ideas.explanation: The cliché that academic prose has to be dull is rejected outright. A paper has to be a delight, sparkling and lively, engaging the mind. The writer has discovered something for the first time in the universe; that excitement should radiate from the page. If the writing was painful and care-filled, the reading will be smooth; if the writer was lazy, the reader will feel it. Most journal-published papers achieve negligible citations and die without trace, partly because not enough passion went into the writing.
core_ideas.quote: If it was not hard to write, it will not be easy to read.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's empirical thumb-rule for modern dissemination. With contemporary tools (working-paper archives, RePEc), about 100,000 people will see the title of a serious paper. About 10,000 will read the abstract. About 1,000 will start reading the body. About 100 will finish. This funnel makes the title the most important sentence in the paper, the abstract the second most important. A well-written paper expands the numbers commensurately; a badly written one dies at every step.
core_ideas.quote: A hundred thousand people are going to read the title of your paper, so make it count.

core_ideas.concept: The Slideshow as Internal Development Platform
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's preferred technique: build the paper first as a 40–50 slide internal deck — gory, intricate, all tables and graphs and citations in linear order. Distinct from a presentation deck. The team brainstorms over it, twenty new ideas surface, the assistant-apprentice goes away to implement them and returns with what she believes is a perfect product. Iterate until the slideshow stops moving — a search process that has converged. Only then does someone turn it into prose. Amit links this to Bezos's anti-PowerPoint memo: superficially they conflict, but Bezos is fighting simplifying decks, while Ajay's slideshow is the opposite — everything-included.
core_ideas.quote: It's a search process that has converged.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's order of operations: first finish the body (field, questions, methods, results), then write the conclusions (why does this matter? downstream consequences? practical applications?), then write the introduction (the thousand-word executive summary), then the abstract, then last of all the title. People constantly suggest cute titles in the middle of the process; save them. You cannot title a paper accurately until you know exactly what the paper is — which often you don't, until you have written it. Tied to Joan Didion: 'I write to find out what I think.'
core_ideas.quote: I write to find out what I think. — Joan Didion

core_ideas.concept: Throw It Away — The Sunk-Cost Fallacy of the Manuscript
core_ideas.explanation: Writing is very, very costly. You have to be willing to change course, willing to throw it away, willing to rewrite. Ajay personally finds it cleaner to delete and rewrite from scratch than to edit a confused chunk. The sunk-cost fallacy of the manuscript — being in love with words because you wrote them — is one of the deepest enemies of clear thought. The basic hygiene: don't be in love with text just because you produced it.
core_ideas.quote: That's a sunk-cost fallacy. We don't give a shit. Throw it away, start over.

core_ideas.concept: Two Pieces of Advice for International Journal Publication
core_ideas.explanation: If you must publish in international journals: first, accept the positioning constraint — they only care about questions they consider interesting and important, so you must mould your work to their map. Second, never attempt large innovations. Peer review chokes on big breaks with the past; if you brought Mendelian genetics to peer reviewers they would throw it out. Journals reward small, incremental, dinky improvements. If you want big moves, you have to operate outside the journal system.
core_ideas.quote: Incremental small papers — big ideas don't work. You're supposed to crawl along with small moves.

core_ideas.concept: Post-Production: Small Rooms Beat Big Conferences
core_ideas.explanation: Once the paper is written, dissemination is non-optional. Write blog articles, write op-eds, make a video of the paper, find conferences. The crucial discovery: 30–40 minutes with 10 attentive people in a small room dwarfs 10 minutes in a 200-person hall. Shallow engagement with large numbers leaves no dent on minds; deep engagement with a few does. This is the same logic as Paul Graham's 'better to be loved by a few than liked by many,' and is also why ten-hour podcasts and one-hour videos exist.
core_ideas.quote: It is far better to get 10 good people in a room... than 10 minutes in front of 200.

core_ideas.concept: The Market Failure of Peer Review
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's view, unsoftened: the peer review system is 'disgusting, terrible — the excellent will always be judged by the mediocre' and no path-breaking insight could ever pass through it. Ajay's softer view: journals today only serve as a credentials system for jobs and grants, not as a dissemination mechanism. Either way, the system that purports to filter for quality is a filter against novelty, and writers should make their peace with that — either play the small-incremental game inside it, or do important work outside it.
core_ideas.quote: The excellent will always be judged by the mediocre.

core_ideas.concept: Be Authentic: Open the Windows of Your House
core_ideas.explanation: Foreign journals will tell Indian researchers their questions are 'not interesting.' Researchers then contort themselves to dress local insights as Western lessons. Ajay rejects this as a sad way to live a life. The alternative is to identify the great questions of the age as you see them in your reality and your lived experience — that is what generates the energy and emotional resilience to chase a question through many setbacks and discover wonderful things, then deliver those jewels to the world.
core_ideas.quote: Open the windows of our house, look out to the real, identify the great questions of the age as we see them in our reality.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's rule for whether to give a talk: am I still enthusiastic about the paper? His own enthusiasm for any one paper decays exponentially. Within a year or two of finishing, he no longer has the level of energy needed to do a great talk on it. His sense of 'what papers I am talking about' shifts as he moves on to the next project. Implication: never do a dull talk, never do a boring talk. If the energy isn't there, don't accept the slot. There are too many stuffed-shirt academics doing dull talks nobody wants to listen to.
core_ideas.quote: Never do a dull talk, never do a boring talk.

core_ideas.concept: It's Hard, It Takes Many Years
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's confession: when young, he grossly underestimated how hard writing a paper would be. Reading papers is much easier than writing one. Like every craft, it takes years of practice, and one of the cruel facts of modern academia is that most freshly minted PhDs are bad at writing papers and don't yet know it. The full capability — to imagine a research project and lead it to completion — requires many post-PhD years of apprenticeship. The journey is long; respect it.
core_ideas.quote: It's a very long childhood, it's a long apprenticeship.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's opening pun: 'Our gentle readers will become gentle writers' — a riff on Amit's signature 'gentle readers.'

Amit on his lifelong handicap: his surname starts with V (so Hayek, Friedman, Keynes and Arrow get top-billing while Verma comes nowhere) and he was born in fucking December — losing both the alphabetical lottery and the Outliers age-group cut-off lottery. 'I had no chance.'

Amit's deadpan riff on Ajay's nightmare scenario for foreign-journal dissemination: 'We could have a party where we call every academic we know and we get them completely drunk and then we gather a bunch of journals and we have a bonfire of the journals.'

Amit's unprompted detour on the Chandrapur tribals: 'There is also the radical possibility that the headgear of the Chandrapur tribals causes global warming.' Ajay, instead of laughing, riffs back deadpan that obscure chemicals in the headgear could trigger atmospheric reactions, prompting Amit's protest: 'I didn't expect you to riff off my immature quip, but continue.'

Amit on the laboriousness of Ajay's process: 'I can imagine after you finished your paper with Ayush and Susan, you're just sitting back and putting on some Joni Mitchell and thinking, what title do we give... and then that brilliant line kind of pops up from the great song Both Sides Now.'
Ajay's gentle dig on small audiences over big ones: 'This is why the universe created ten-hour podcasts and one-hour videos.'

Amit's mock-conspiracy theory about alphabetical authorship: 'Where is a Zimbalist? There's no great economist called Zimbalist. Where are the Nobel Prizes to people whose names begin with Y? Name one.' Ajay agrees it would make a paper: count the first letters of all econ Nobel laureates' surnames and test for statistical significance against the population distribution.

Karl Marx's epitaph: 'The philosophers have hitherto only interpreted the world; the point, however, is to change it.' — invoked by Ajay as the spirit of action-oriented research projects, distinct from purely understanding-oriented ones.

Joan Didion: 'I write to find out what I think.' — used by Amit to defend the position that you cannot fully outline a paper top-down before writing it; the writing itself shapes what the writing turns out to be.
Blaise Pascal: 'I'm sorry this letter is so long, I did not have time to make it short.' — Amit's gloss on the asymmetry between the cost of writing concisely and the cost of writing at all.

Georges Simenon: the key theme of all his novels is that 'no two people can ever communicate with each other.' — Amit's anchor for why writing is hard: you and the reader are never quite in the same room.
The apocryphal apple-on-Newton's-head story — invoked as the archetype of a research narrative that is fun but is not the paper. The paper is what you found, not the falling fruit.

Jeff Bezos's anti-PowerPoint memo at Amazon: instead of slides, write proper paragraphs over a fixed number of pages, distributed in advance. Amit invokes it to distinguish Bezos's 'simplifying' deck (banned) from Ajay's 'gory' development deck (recommended).
Paul Graham: 'Better to be loved by a few than liked by many.' — Amit's frame for Ajay's preference for small intense conferences over large impersonal ones.
Ignaz Semmelweis, Gregor Mendel and Charles Darwin invoked as canonical victims-or-bypassers of peer review. 'Or Darwin for that matter, unless Wallace was his peer.' — Amit's deadpan caveat.
'The Rising Price of Husbands' — Bijou Rao's 1990s paper on dowry, held up by Amit as the model of a clever title that is also accurately about the paper.
